questions.q: What is the name of the EU’s common currency, and how many member states currently use it?
questions.a: The common currency is the euro, used by 20 of the 27 EU member states (the “eurozone”). A wrong answer (e.g., “all 27 use the euro” or “the currency is the pound”) reveals confusion between EU membership and eurozone membership, and ignorance of the opt‑outs negotiated by Denmark and (formerly) the UK.

questions.q: Explain why the EU is described as a “supranational” organisation rather than a mere intergovernmental alliance like ASEAN.
questions.a: The EU has institutions (Commission, Court of Justice, Parliament) that can make binding laws directly applicable in member states without further national ratification, and its law has supremacy over national law in agreed areas. A wrong answer that equates EU with ASEAN (where decisions are non‑binding and require consensus) shows the student misses the unique legal character of EU integration — the core of its political power.

questions.q: A small Indian textile firm wants to export to Germany and France. Identify which EU institution sets the common external tariff the firm will face, and which EU body negotiates the trade agreement that could lower that tariff.
questions.a: The common external tariff is set by the **Council of the EU** (on Commission proposal) as part of the Common Commercial Policy. Trade agreements are negotiated by the **European Commission** (DG Trade) on a mandate from the Council. A wrong answer naming the European Parliament as the negotiator (it only approves/rejects final deals) or the WTO (which only provides the framework) indicates the student cannot map EU competences to real‑world trade scenarios.

questions.q: Compare the EU’s decision‑making in economic policy (e.g., single market rules) with its decision‑making in foreign policy (CFSP). Why does the latter remain largely intergovernmental?
questions.a: Economic policy uses Qualified Majority Voting (QMV) in the Council and co‑decision with Parliament, allowing supranational action. CFSP requires **unanimity** in the Council, giving each member a veto, and the Commission has only a supporting role. A wrong answer claiming QMV applies to CFSP ignores the deliberate design to keep sovereignty over war/peace issues with national capitals — a key limit on EU political power.

questions.q: Assess the claim: “The EU is a global economic giant but a political dwarf.” Use two pieces of evidence from the last decade to support or refute it.
questions.a: The claim is partially valid but outdated. Evidence for “economic giant”: EU is the world’s largest single market (GDP ~$18 trillion) and top trading bloc. Evidence against “political dwarf”: EU led the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA, 2015), imposes sanctions on Russia (2014, 2022) with global effect, and drives global climate policy (European Green Deal, CBAM). A wrong answer that only cites economic data or only cites failures (e.g., Libya 2011) shows inability to weigh mixed evidence — a key evaluative skill.

questions.q: Draft a one‑paragraph proposal for a new EU policy that would strengthen its role as a “normative power” in the Indo‑Pacific, specifying which EU institution would initiate it and which decision‑making procedure would apply.
questions.a: A strong answer proposes, e.g., an “EU‑Indo‑Pacific Connectivity Partnership” for sustainable infrastructure, initiated by the **European Commission** under the **ordinary legislative procedure** (co‑decision) if it falls under development cooperation/trade, or under **CFSP unanimity** if framed as a strategic security initiative. A weak answer ignores the institutional initiator or the voting rule, revealing the student cannot link policy ideas to EU’s actual constitutional architecture.
